attributes.origin: Douala, in the 20th century. Sources differ on the exact decade.
attributes.name_meaning: Means (I) dance in the Douala language.
attributes.roots: Grew out of the Douala kossa dance and drew on ambasse bey, assiko, highlife, Congolese rumba and merengue.
attributes.early_figures: Emmanuel Nelle Eyoum used the refrain kossa kossa with his group Los Calvinos. In the mid-1960s Eboa Lotin played an early form on harmonica and guitar.
attributes.milestones: Had a wave of mainstream success across Africa in the 1980s. Manu Dibango's Soul Makossa came out in 1972. Shakira sampled the Golden Sounds song Zamina mina (Zangalewa) for the 2010 World Cup.
attributes.related_style: Makassi is a lighter style of makossa.

source.citation: Wikipedia, Music of Cameroon (CC BY-SA 4.0), and the Radiodiffusion Internasionaal blog. Compiled for this collection and not yet reviewed by a second person.

attributes.origin: Centre Region, around Yaoundé, among the Beti (Ewondo) people.
attributes.description: A native folk music based on a war rhythm, played by three to five balafon players with other percussion.
attributes.history: Migration to Yaoundé helped spread it. By the 1970s performers had added brass instruments and more explicit lyrics.
attributes.notable_group: Les Têtes Brulées became a well-known export, especially after accompanying the national football team to the 1990 and 1994 World Cups.
attributes.relationship: Seen as a rival to the more urban makossa of Douala.

attributes.origin: A folk rhythm of the Bassa people.
attributes.description: A local variant of palm wine music. Makossa can sound like a slowed-down assiko.
attributes.styles: Hard, fast assiko among the Bassa and Eton, a cooler assiko among the Bulu, and the bottle dance of the Northwest Region.

attributes.origin: Late 19th century, in German Kamerun. It began among the Yabassi people and became popular in Douala after the Second World War.
attributes.description: Folk music and dance based on guitar, with sticks and bottles for percussion. It is faster than assiko.
attributes.legacy: A precursor of makossa. Sallé John helped revive it.

attributes.origin: A style of the West Region, especially among the Bangangté people.
attributes.artists: Pierre Didy Tchakounté, André Marie Talla and the group Kouchouam Mbada are associated with it.
